roll_call: I was Japan's 124th emperor, reigning from my accession in 1926 through war, defeat, occupation, and until 1989.
In December 1941, the Imperial Rescript declaring war on the United States and Britain was promulgated in my name and bore my signature. The war was waged in my name.
In August 1945, I decided to accept the Potsdam Declaration and broadcast my voice for the first time to tell the nation the war would end.
deploy: Leave no more cities and people on the battlefield. Accept the Potsdam Declaration and lay down your arms.
Approving decisions submitted by ministers does not transfer responsibility to the ministers. An order issued in my name is also my responsibility.
Stop any attempt to defy surrender and plunge the country into internal fighting. Loyalty that demands more war will only kill more people.
battle_win: The decision to end the war prevented further deaths. The merit of ordering an end does not erase responsibility for approving its beginning.
Under the postwar Constitution, the emperor became a symbol rather than a ruler. The people and their government built democracy and recovery.
My biological research remains in hydrozoan specimens and taxonomic records. Verifiable specimens, not a crown, were the standard of judgment.
battle_draw: The military and cabinet exerted heavy pressure, and convention constrained how my authority was used. That does not mean I had no authority.
Both the 1941 declaration of war and the 1945 rescript ending the war bear my signature. The final document cannot close responsibility for everything between them.
The 1946 rescript said the emperor's bond with the people did not rest on myth and legend. It did not answer the question of wartime responsibility.
battle_lose: The Japanese military invaded China and lands across Asia and the Pacific in my name, and countless civilians and soldiers died. My silence cannot escape that outcome.
My voice in the surrender broadcast came far too late. It could not restore the ruined cities or the lives taken in the colonies.
I was not prosecuted as a war criminal and remained on the throne. That was a choice of occupation policy, not a verdict of innocence.
clash_attack: Do not hide those who gave orders behind the word loyalty. If people fought in my name, my responsibility must be recorded too.
Do not dress defeat only in the virtue of sacrifice. First say who invaded and who paid the price.
The decision to end the war cannot erase the decision to begin it. My final decision was no acquittal for my first approval.

roll_call: I became emperor in 1926 and lived through war, defeat, and occupation.
I signed the 1941 rescript declaring war on the United States and Britain.
In August 1945, I announced the surrender by radio.
deploy: Accept the Potsdam Declaration and lay down your arms.
Do not blame my ministers for orders issued in my name.
Stop the soldiers who would resist surrender. More fighting will only kill people.
battle_win: By choosing surrender, I prevented further deaths. My responsibility for starting the war remains.
After the war, I lost sovereign power and remained a symbol. The people rebuilt Japan.
I studied hydrozoans and left specimens and taxonomic records.
battle_draw: The military pressured me, but I was not without authority.
I signed both the war and surrender rescripts. The end does not erase the beginning.
In 1946, I denied the emperor's divinity. Responsibility for the war remained.
battle_lose: Japan invaded in my name. I cannot escape responsibility for the dead.
The surrender broadcast came too late. It could not undo colonial suffering or ruined cities.
I was never tried as a war criminal. That was not an acquittal.
clash_attack: Do not hide commanders behind loyalty!
Ending the war does not erase starting it!

roll_call: Later generations called me Prince Shōtoku, but most accounts of my deeds come from the Nihon Shoki, compiled in 720 about a century after my death.
The Nihon Shoki says I assisted Empress Suiko and established the twelve court ranks and the seventeen articles. It is not a contemporary text in my own hand.
The Book of Sui records an envoy and state letter from Wa in 607, but it does not name me as the letter's author.
deploy: Do not let one person decide great matters. Consult many people to avoid a mistaken conclusion.
Those who hear lawsuits must reject profit and judge impartially. Do not let only the rich man's plea pass like a stone through water.
Set private motives aside and turn toward public affairs. Resentment destroys both harmony and law.
battle_win: The Book of Sui records twelve court ranks in Wa. It is one of the rare outside records that aligns with the later tradition in the Nihon Shoki.
In 607, an envoy from Wa told the Sui court that dozens of monks had come to study Buddhism. The exchange across the sea remains in the record.
The final article says important matters should be discussed with many people. Harmony meant deliberation, not only obedience.
battle_draw: The seventeen articles appear in the Nihon Shoki under the year 604, but the surviving text depends on a chronicle compiled in 720. My direct authorship cannot be assumed.
The letter from the ruler where the sun rises survives in the Book of Sui, but it does not name me as author. The diplomatic event and the writer's identity must remain distinct.
The Sangyō Gisho is traditionally attributed to me, but its manuscripts and authorship remain subjects of scholarly debate.
battle_lose: The claim that I heard ten people at once is a marvelous tale in the Nihon Shoki. It should not be repeated as contemporary fact.
Later veneration enlarged the image of me as the sole author of every reform. It cannot erase the roles of Empress Suiko, Soga no Umako, and the court.
For institutions attributed to me, few original texts or implementation records survive. This is an age in which evidence is scarcer than famous names.
clash_attack: Do not turn harmony into silence. The seventeen articles also say that important matters must be discussed by many.
Do not let a powerful man's bribe block the poor man's lawsuit. A court that reverses stone and water is not order.
Do not state tradition as fact. Separate the Nihon Shoki's record, the Book of Sui's outside testimony, and later devotion.

roll_call: Later generations called me Prince Shōtoku. Most records were written much later.
Tradition says I assisted Empress Suiko and established the twelve ranks and seventeen articles.
The Book of Sui records the 607 envoy, but not the letter's author.
deploy: Do not decide great matters alone. Consult others.
Reject bribes and hear the poor as fairly as the rich.
Put private resentment aside and serve the public good.
battle_win: The Book of Sui also records Wa's twelve court ranks.
In 607, envoys and monks crossed to Sui seeking knowledge.
The seventeen articles say great matters require consultation.
battle_draw: The seventeen articles survive only in the later Nihon Shoki. My authorship cannot be proved.
The letter from the land of the rising sun survives, but no record names me as author.
The Sangyō Gisho is attributed to me, but its manuscripts and authorship remain disputed.
battle_lose: The story that I heard ten people at once is a later legend.
I did not reform the court alone. Empress Suiko and her court shared the work.
Most original texts and implementation records for my reforms are lost.
clash_attack: Do not use harmony to silence people!
Do not take bribes and silence the poor!
Do not put your words in my mouth!
